facts.fact_text: On 11 August 2012 the applicant informed the local police in Kharkiv of his intention to hold a peaceful assembly under the banner of 'Ukraine for fair elections'.
The applicant's intended assembly was planned to run from 12 August 2012 onwards for an indefinite period of time.
The applicant's intended assembly was planned to be held in Shevchenko Park in Kharkiv city centre.
There is no information as to whether the applicant actually attempted to hold the demonstration on 12 August 2012 as he declared to the authorities.
On 13 August 2012 the Executive Committee of the Kharkiv City Council decided that the assembly that the applicant planned to hold should not be permitted.
On 13 August 2012 the Kharkiv District Administrative Court allowed the Executive Committee of the Kharkiv City Council's request and prohibited the applicant's planned assembly.
On 17 September 2012 the Kharkiv Administrative Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal against the prohibition of the planned assembly.
On 15 November 2012 the Higher Administrative Court rejected a request by the applicant for leave to appeal on points of law.

The Kharkiv District Administrative Court noted that the matters under examination were regulated by the Temporary Regulations on the procedure for organising and holding meetings, rallies, street marches and demonstrations in the city of Kharkiv.

The Kharkiv District Administrative Court noted that the Temporary Regulations on the procedure for organising and holding meetings, rallies, street marches and demonstrations in the city of Kharkiv were binding under section 73 of the Local Self-Government in Ukraine Act.

Article 92 of the Constitution of Ukraine provides that human and citizens' rights and freedoms, the guarantees of these rights and freedoms, and the main duties of the citizen shall be determined exclusively by the laws of Ukraine.

Section 73 § 1 of the Local Self-Government in Ukraine Act, 1997, provides that acts of the council, mayor, or the executive committee of the city council which are adopted within the limits of the powers granted to them shall be binding on all executive authorities located in the relevant territory, associations of citizens, enterprises, institutions and organisations, and officials, as well as citizens permanently or temporarily residing in the relevant territory.
Decision no. 543 of the Executive Committee of the Kharkiv City Council of 6 June 2007 introduced the procedure for organising peaceful gatherings in the city of Kharkiv.
Decision no. 543 of the Executive Committee of the Kharkiv City Council of 6 June 2007 was adopted on the basis of section 38 and section 59 § 6 of the Local Self-Government in Ukraine Act, 1997.

The Temporary Regulations approved by Decision no. 543 of the Executive Committee of the Kharkiv City Council of 6 June 2007 state in their General Provisions that they had been drawn up in accordance with the Convention, the Local Self-Government in Ukraine Act, the Decree of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR of 28 July 1988 on the procedure for organising and holding meetings, rallies, street marches and demonstrations in the USSR, the decision of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine of 19 April 2001 in a case regarding timely notification of a peaceful assembly, and the Code of Administrative Justice.

Under the Temporary Regulations approved by Decision no. 543 of the Executive Committee of the Kharkiv City Council of 6 June 2007, notification of the intended event was to be submitted in writing and in good time, that is, not less than ten days prior to the planned date of holding the event.

The Temporary Regulations approved by Decision no. 543 of the Executive Committee of the Kharkiv City Council of 6 June 2007 provided that the holding of mass gatherings within parks and other recreational areas was not permitted, except in one particular park, namely Molodizhnyi.

The Temporary Regulations approved by Decision no. 543 of the Executive Committee of the Kharkiv City Council of 6 June 2007 provided that the simultaneous holding of any mass gatherings in a location where other mass events had been authorised was not permitted.

The Temporary Regulations approved by Decision no. 543 of the Executive Committee of the Kharkiv City Council of 6 June 2007 provided that the holding of any demonstrations and pickets directly in front of the offices of institutions and organisations where this would interfere with the work of those institutions and organisations or would impede members of the public from visiting them was not permitted.

The Temporary Regulations approved by Decision no. 543 of the Executive Committee of the Kharkiv City Council of 6 June 2007 provided that the holding of mass gatherings prior to 8 a.m. or after 10 p.m. was not permitted.

The October 2016 Joint Opinion noted that in the absence of clear legislative regulations on freedom of assembly, local authorities in Ukraine have issued specific and widely varying local rules in order to regulate the exercise of the right to freedom of assembly.

The October 2016 Joint Opinion noted that according to certain civil society organisations, regulation of the right to freedom of assembly by local decisions is a widespread practice in Ukraine, which would contradict Article 92 of the Constitution of Ukraine, which provides that human and citizens' rights and freedoms are determined exclusively by the laws of Ukraine.

The Kharkiv District Administrative Court based its decision to ban the assembly on the ground that the applicant had chosen the city centre as the location for the assembly, not far from areas with significant levels of road traffic.

The Kharkiv District Administrative Court based its decision to ban the assembly on the ground that the proposed location of the assembly was a place where the people of Kharkiv liked to rest and take part in leisure activities.
The Kharkiv District Administrative Court noted that the assembly could pose a risk to the health and life of the inhabitants of Kharkiv, as well as their right to move about safely in the city.

The Kharkiv Administrative Court of Appeal noted that the holding of the applicant's assembly at the same time and place as the Honey Fair and the Flower Show could lead to a breach of public order and a threat to safety, because the applicant's assembly could spontaneously be joined by an unknown number of people.

The Kharkiv Administrative Court of Appeal noted that if the applicant's assembly were spontaneously joined by additional people, the number of participants would increase and the assembly would become unmanageable, all of which would hinder the movement of people and vehicles.

Article 39 of the Constitution of Ukraine provides that restrictions on the exercise of the right to peaceful assembly may be established by a court in accordance with the law, in the interests of national security and public order only, for the purpose of preventing disturbances or crimes, protecting the health of the population, or protecting the rights and freedoms of other persons.

Article 182 § 5 of the Code of Administrative Justice, 2005, as worded at the material time, provides that the court shall allow the claimant's claims in the interests of national security and public order where it establishes that the holding of gatherings, meetings, rallies, demonstrations or other assemblies may create a real risk of disturbances or crime, or endanger the health of the population or the rights and freedoms of other people, and that in its ruling the court shall indicate the manner in which the exercise of the right to peaceful assembly is to be restricted.

Under the Temporary Regulations approved by Decision no. 543 of the Executive Committee of the Kharkiv City Council of 6 June 2007, freedom of assembly could be restricted by a court in the interests of national security and public safety, for considerations of public health, for the prevention of crime and disorder, and for the protection of the rights of others.
The Kharkiv District Administrative Court based its decision to ban the assembly on the ground that the notice sent by the applicant did not provide clear details of the assembly.

The Kharkiv District Administrative Court based its decision to ban the assembly on the ground that the notice had not been sent a reasonable time in advance, noting that it was dated 11 August 2012 and had been received by the Kharkiv City Council on 13 August 2012, whereas the assembly had been scheduled for 12 August 2012.
The Kharkiv District Administrative Court based its decision to ban the assembly on the ground that the applicant planned to hold an assembly for an indefinite period of time.

The Kharkiv District Administrative Court based its decision to ban the assembly on the ground that the applicant had chosen the city centre as the location for the assembly, not far from areas with significant levels of road traffic.

The Kharkiv District Administrative Court based its decision to ban the assembly on the ground that the proposed location of the assembly was a place where the people of Kharkiv liked to rest and take part in leisure activities.
The Kharkiv District Administrative Court noted that 'there was no evidence to prove that the assembly was not contrary to the interests of the inhabitants of Kharkiv'.
The Kharkiv District Administrative Court noted that the assembly could pose a risk to the health and life of the inhabitants of Kharkiv, as well as their right to move about safely in the city.

The Kharkiv District Administrative Court stated that 'the material in the case file [did] not demonstrate that there [was] no possibility of a violation of the rights and freedoms of people [not participating in the assembly]'.

The Kharkiv Administrative Court of Appeal noted that the time and place of the applicant's planned assembly coincided with the time and place of the Honey Fair and the Flower Show, which were to take place from 14 to 23 August 2012 in Shevchenko Park.

The Kharkiv Administrative Court of Appeal noted that the holding of the applicant's assembly at the same time and place as the Honey Fair and the Flower Show could lead to a breach of public order and a threat to safety, because the applicant's assembly could spontaneously be joined by an unknown number of people.

The Kharkiv Administrative Court of Appeal noted that if the applicant's assembly were spontaneously joined by additional people, the number of participants would increase and the assembly would become unmanageable, all of which would hinder the movement of people and vehicles.
